german.label: Germany
bound: Cincinnati in Ohio, where a brother keeps a bakery
a farm in Iowa, bought on paper
Philadelphia, and then west into Pennsylvania
Kansas, where the railway sells land cheap
why: the farm was too small to split among four sons
two bad harvests, and a debt at the savings bank
since the war the eldest would serve seven years in the army and five more in the reserve
a brother in Ohio writes that there is land for anyone who works
the weaving in the village went to the factories, and the wages with it
german.speech: You speak English as a German farmer who learned a little from a phrasebook on the train: short careful sentences, now and then the verb at the end ('Tomorrow we to the ship go'), many pleases and thank-yous.
greet: Good day, good day. You are from this city, yes?
Ah, a young man. Please, it is here the boats to the big ship come?
Good day. We wait for the ship. Always we wait.

swiss.label: Switzerland
regions: the Emmental, in the canton of Bern
bound: New Glarus in Wisconsin, where cousins keep cows
Ohio, to a cheese maker from the next valley
Missouri, where the land is cheap
why: the cheese fell in price and the farm went with it
the parish paid half the fare, to have one family less on the poor box
the spinning mill in the valley shut its doors
cousins in Wisconsin write that the grass is good and nobody owns it yet
swiss.speech: You speak English slowly, a word at a time, and apologise for it; you are proud, tidy and careful with money.
greet: Good day to you. Please speak slow, my English is from a little book.
Good day. It is very flat here. At home the mountains stand up to the sky.
Good day. We are the family from the mountains, you see.

dutch.label: the Netherlands
why: the landlord raised the rent after the potato rot
our church stands apart from the old one, and the village never forgave us
an uncle in Michigan sent the fare in a letter
there is no land to buy at home, not for money we will ever have
dutch.speech: You speak plain careful English with a Dutch tongue, and are glad a Fleming half understands you; you say 'yes, yes' when you are thinking.
greet: Good day. Yes, yes, we are for America.
Good day, young man. You are a Fleming? Then we almost understand each other.
Good day. The quay is big, the ship is bigger.

belgian.label: Belgium
regions: the country round Wavre, in Brabant
bound: Green Bay in Wisconsin, where the Walloons are
why: the flax work is gone, and the linen with it
letters from Wisconsin were read out at the church door, and half the parish talks of nothing else
the farm goes to the eldest brother, and there is nothing for the rest of us
belgian.speech: You are a country person from the far side of Belgium: slow, shy of the big city, better at French than at Flemish; plain words.
greet: Good day. We are from the country, you see. This city is too big.
Good day. You are from the Kempen? No, we are from further off.
Good day, young man. Is it always so loud here?

bohemian.label: Bohemia
bound: Chicago, to the Bohemians on the west side
why: no land of our own, only day work on the estate
the army wanted the eldest son
a man from the next village came back from America with a gold watch
bohemian.speech: You know only a handful of English words and use them bravely, with long pauses and your hands.
greet: Good day. You know, please, when the ship goes?
Good day. Sorry, my words are few.
Good... good day. America, yes. Soon.

hungarian.label: Upper Hungary
why: the land gives nothing, and a man back from the mines had money in his pockets
the lord's steward took the best field
the eldest must go for a soldier, and we would rather go all together to America
hungarian.speech: You have very little English: short words, many pauses, a smile when you are lost; you understand more than you can say.
greet: Good... good day. English, a little. Very little.
Day, sir. The ship? Today? No? Tomorrow.
Good day. We go far, far. America.

fears: the sea, and the weeks below deck
sickness on board: they say the ship fever takes the little ones first
being cheated before we even leave; everybody here wants our money
that the money runs out before the land is found
that the children forget their prayers and their mother tongue
not understanding a word over there
that the brother's letters were too kind about America
lostAt: by the door of the Hessenatie
at the foot of the crane

policePost.label: the police post by the town hall

labels.sentry: soldier of the line, on guard
labels.navvy: labourer of the town's works, pulling down the old wall

labels.post_clerk: clerk of the post and telegraph office
labels.velo_maker: velocipede maker, a smith who builds and hires out velocipedes
labels.wheelwright: wheelwright, who builds and hires out handcarts
labels.lodging_keeper: keeper of the emigrants' lodging house
labels.beadle: beadle of the cathedral (the suisse, who keeps order at mass)
labels.chair_woman: chair woman of the cathedral (she lets the chairs at mass)
labels.registrar: clerk of the civil registry at the town hall
labels.alderman: alderman of the civil registry, who marries couples at the town hall
labels.cellar_master: cellar master of Peyrot's wine warehouse in the Vleeshuis
labels.cellarman: cellarman at Peyrot's wine warehouse in the Vleeshuis
labels.painter: painter with a studio in the Vleeshuis
labels.attendant: attendant of the Museum of Antiquities in the Steen
labels.storekeeper: storekeeper of the State warehouse in the Oostershuis
labels.milk_woman: milk woman with a dog cart
labels.baker_boy: baker's boy with the bread cart
labels.devotion_seller: keeper of a stall against the cathedral (rosaries, candles, holy pictures)
labels.nun: Black Sister, who nurses the sick at home
labels.tourist: English traveller come to see the Rubens paintings
labels.fence: dealer in odds and ends, after dark
labels.nightcarter: carter who works by night and asks no questions
labels.cracksman: a man in a dark coat who needs a lookout
labels.colonial: grocer in colonial goods (coffee, tea, sugar, spices)
labels.washerwoman: washerwoman, who washes for the better houses at the court pump
labels.loafer: lad out of work who hangs about a street corner with his mates
labels.watchman: night watchman of the back streets
labels.doctor: physician, on his rounds of the back streets
labels.drunkard: docker out of work, too fond of the jenever
labels.miller: miller of a mill on the town wall
labels.miller_man: miller's man, who carries the sacks and drives the mill's cart
